name: Plank and side plank
noEquipmentAlternative: No equipment needed; use a folded towel or bedsheet under the forearms instead of a mat on hard floors.

metOptions.activity: MET: 2.8, 2024 Adult Compendium of Physical Activities, code 02024, "calisthenics (e.g., curl-ups, abdominal crunches, plank), light effort". The 2024 entry names the plank directly.
Note: some calculators use 3.5 METs (code 02030, general light-to-moderate calisthenics) for planks. FitPlate uses 02024 because it names the plank.

setupSteps: Clear a strip of floor about 2 m x 1 m (est.). Move the coffee table away from your head end.
Lay the mat lengthwise. On a hard floor, add a folded towel where your elbows will go.
Lie face down on the mat.
Place your elbows on the floor directly under your shoulders. ACE describes elbows close to the sides and directly under the shoulders.

Lay your forearms flat, pointing forward and parallel (shoulder-width apart). Palms can face down or face each other with fists loosely closed. Both are common; pick whichever is kinder to your wrists.
Tuck your toes under so the balls of your feet are on the floor.
Feet: hip-width apart is easier to balance; feet together is harder. Beginners start hip-width.
Look at the floor just in front of your hands so the neck stays in line with the spine.
Use the same mat, turned so your body lies along it.

Lie on your right side, legs straight and stacked (left foot on top of right). Beginners can instead place the top foot on the floor in front of the bottom foot (staggered feet). This is easier to balance.

Prop yourself on your right forearm. Put your right elbow directly under your right shoulder, with the forearm pointing forward, at right angles to your body. ACE's modified version uses a 90-degree elbow.
Rest your left hand on your left hip, or on the floor in front of your chest for balance.
Check that your head, shoulders, hips and feet are in one line, as if you were lying against a wall behind you.
Knee version (start here if new): bend both knees so your feet are behind you. Harvard Health uses knees bent to 90 degrees. The body line is then head to knees.

steps.title: Set the shoulders
steps.action: Gently press your forearms into the floor so your chest lifts slightly away from the floor between your shoulder blades.
steps.feel: The upper back widens; the shoulders do not sink toward the ears.
steps.visualCheck: Side: shoulder is stacked directly above the elbow. Front: forearms parallel, shoulders level.

steps.title: Brace the stomach
steps.action: Tighten your stomach as if you were about to be poked in the belly. Do not suck it in.
steps.feel: A firm ring of tension around the waist.
steps.breathing: Breathe out gently as you brace.
steps.visualCheck: The belly does not visibly bulge outward.

steps.title: Squeeze the buttocks and thighs
steps.action: Squeeze your buttocks and straighten your knees by tightening the front of your thighs.
steps.feel: Your hips feel locked; the lower back does not feel pinched.
steps.visualCheck: Kneecaps lift slightly off the floor even before the body rises.

steps.title: Lift the body
steps.action: Push through your forearms and toes and lift your hips, thighs and knees off the floor all at once, like a single plank of wood.
steps.feel: Weight shared between the forearms and toes; work in the stomach and front of the shoulders.
steps.visualCheck: Side: a straight line from the back of the head through the shoulders, hips and heels. Hips are neither higher than the shoulders nor dipping below the line. Front: hips level, not twisted.

steps.title: Hold
steps.action: Stay still and keep all the tension from steps 1–3.
steps.feel: The stomach working hard, with no ache or pinch in the lower back.
steps.breathing: Slow, steady breaths through the nose or mouth. Never hold your breath (holding the breath raises blood pressure further during isometric work).
steps.visualCheck: Side: line stays straight; head does not drop or crane up. Front: elbows still under shoulders, shoulder blades not winging out.

steps.title: Lower
steps.action: Lower your knees to the floor first, then your hips and chest.

steps.title: Rest
steps.action: Rest face down or move to child's pose.

steps.part: B. Side plank (right side shown; repeat on the left)
steps.title: Line up
steps.action: From the setup position, check that the right elbow is under the right shoulder and the body is in one line.
steps.feel: Weight on the forearm and the side of the bottom foot (or bottom knee).
steps.visualCheck: Front: head, chest, hips and feet in one line. Side: the body does not lean forward or back.

steps.part: B. Side plank (right side shown; repeat on the left)
steps.title: Brace
steps.action: Tighten your stomach as in plank step 2.
steps.feel: Firm waist, especially on the floor side.
steps.visualCheck: No visible change other than slight firming.

steps.part: B. Side plank (right side shown; repeat on the left)
steps.title: Lift the hips
steps.action: Press the forearm and the side of the bottom foot (or knee) into the floor and lift your hips until your body is straight from head to feet (or knees).
steps.feel: The side of the waist on the floor side working; the side of the bottom hip working.
steps.visualCheck: Front: a straight line from head to feet; the hip does not sag toward the floor or pike up. Side: the top hip stays directly over the bottom hip (no rolling forward or backward).

steps.part: B. Side plank (right side shown; repeat on the left)
steps.title: Push the floor away
steps.action: Press the forearm down so the bottom shoulder does not collapse toward the ear.
steps.feel: Muscles around the bottom shoulder blade working.
steps.visualCheck: A clear gap between the bottom ear and the bottom shoulder.

steps.part: B. Side plank (right side shown; repeat on the left)
steps.title: Hold
steps.feel: The side abs and side hip working; no pain in the bottom shoulder or lower back.
steps.breathing: Slow, steady breaths. Do not hold your breath.
steps.tempo: Beginners 8–10 seconds per hold, repeated (see section 7).
steps.visualCheck: Same as step 3; the top arm (if raised) points straight up.

steps.part: B. Side plank (right side shown; repeat on the left)
steps.title: Lower
steps.action: Lower the hip back to the mat with control.
steps.breathing: Breathe in as you lower (ACE cue).

steps.part: B. Side plank (right side shown; repeat on the left)
steps.title: Switch sides
steps.action: Roll onto your front, then onto the other side, and repeat steps 1–6. Do the same number and length of holds on each side.

commonMistakes.title: Lower back sagging (plank) or hip dropping (side plank)
commonMistakes.text: Lower back sagging (plank) or hip dropping (side plank). Why: the work shifts from the trunk muscles onto the lower back joints, and it can strain the back. Fix: tighten the belly and squeeze the buttocks; if it keeps happening, end the hold or drop to the knee version (ACE advises dropping to the knees when the back starts to dip).

commonMistakes.title: Hips piked high
commonMistakes.text: Hips piked high. Why: it makes the hold easier and takes work away from the abs. Fix: lower the hips until the body is a straight line; check a side-view video.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath. Why: breath-holding during isometric effort causes extra, sharp rises in blood pressure and can cause dizziness. Fix: count breaths out loud or breathe steadily through the nose.

commonMistakes.title: Shoulders sinking or elbows in the wrong spot
commonMistakes.text: Shoulders sinking or elbows in the wrong spot. Why: the shoulder joint takes load it is not set up for, and shoulder blades may wing. Fix: elbows directly under shoulders; push the floor away.

commonMistakes.title: Chasing long times with poor form
commonMistakes.text: Chasing long times with poor form. Why: once form breaks, the hold is no longer training the target muscles well, and some experts (McGill) argue long single holds add little for the average person. Fix: stop the hold when form breaks; use repeated short holds instead.

commonMistakes.title: Head craning up to watch a phone or TV
commonMistakes.text: Head craning up to watch a phone or TV. Why: strains the neck. Fix: put the phone timer on the floor under your face.

commonMistakes.title: Side plank: hips rolling forward or backward
commonMistakes.text: Side plank: hips rolling forward or backward. Why: the obliques and side hip work less and the lower back twists. Fix: stack the top hip directly over the bottom hip; imagine your back against a wall.

commonMistakes.title: Only training one side harder
commonMistakes.text: Only training one side harder. Why: McGill-style testing aims for left and right side bridge times to be within about 5% of each other (right:left ratio 0.95–1.05 in the ACE protocol). Fix: always match time and holds on both sides.

safetyNotes: Back problems: many back-care programmes (McGill's Big Three) use the side bridge, but people with acute low-back pain, a recent flare-up or recent back surgery should get professional advice first. ACE lists low-back pain, recent back surgery and acute flare-ups as reasons the side bridge test may not suit someone.
Shoulder problems: both holds load the shoulder on the floor. ACE notes shoulder pain or weakness as a reason to avoid the side bridge test. Use the wall plank and stop with any shoulder pain.
Wrist problems: the forearm version avoids loading the wrist; keep hands relaxed.

High blood pressure: a single isometric hold can briefly raise blood pressure, more so with breath-holding. Breathe continuously, keep holds short, and anyone with uncontrolled or severe high blood pressure should get medical clearance first.

Pregnancy and after childbirth (including diastasis recti, a gap between the two halves of the six-pack muscle): no ACOG or other authoritative plank-specific guidance was found (Not found). Fitness sources commonly suggest wall, counter or knee versions, and stopping if the belly domes or bulges. Seek advice from a doctor or women's-health physiotherapist.
Recent abdominal surgery or hernia: avoid until cleared by your surgeon.
Knee problems (knee versions): pad the knees with a folded towel.
